title: Classic Vinaigrette
subtitle: sharp, balanced French salad dressing
excerpt: A good vinaigrette is one of the most useful things in a cook's repertoire. This version uses sherry vinegar and Dijon mustard for a dressing that clings to leaves rather than sliding off. The ratio is 3 parts oil to 1 part vinegar. Everything else is seasoning.
sourceNotes: The French vinaigrette is the foundation of French salad dressing. The classic ratio of 3:1 oil to vinegar appears in French cookbooks from the 19th century onwards.

recipe.batchNotes: Make a larger batch and keep in a jar in the fridge for up to 2 weeks. Shake before using.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Keeps in the fridge for 2 weeks. Shake or whisk before serving.

content.text: The mustard is the emulsifier. It helps the oil and vinegar stay combined rather than separating immediately. Do not skip it. If you want a different flavour, use red wine vinegar or white wine vinegar instead of sherry vinegar.
Put the mustard, honey, salt, and vinegar in a bowl. Whisk to combine.
Add the olive oil in a slow, steady stream, whisking constantly until the dressing is combined and slightly thickened.
Taste and adjust with more salt, vinegar, or honey as needed.
Store in a jar and shake before using. Dress salads just before serving.

items.cause: Not enough mustard or not whisked enough
items.fix: Add a little more mustard and whisk again.
Whisk in a little more oil. Add a touch more honey to balance.

content.text: Vinaigrette is the standard French salad dressing and has been for at least 200 years. The 3:1 ratio of oil to acid is a guideline, not a rule -- adjust it to the sharpness of your vinegar and the leaves you are dressing. Sherry vinegar gives a rounded flavour; red wine vinegar is sharper; white wine vinegar is the most neutral.
